title: Weekly electronic symptom reporting during chemotherapy: who stops reporting, why, and what happens to alerts
subtitle: Two candidate designs: a pragmatic trial in the clinics yet to start, or a mixed methods evaluation of the rollout
statement: Weekly electronic symptom reporting between chemotherapy cycles started in two clinics in March 2026 and reaches two more in January 2027. Completion is patchy, some severe-symptom alerts wait over weekends, and older patients report stopping because nobody seemed to read their answers. The centre needs to know whether the programme reaches the patients it is meant to help, who stops reporting and why, and how alerts are handled, before it is extended; the design is not yet chosen.
whoAffected: Adults receiving chemotherapy in the regional cancer centre, especially older patients, people without home internet and those needing an interpreter; triage nurses who read alerts; families who support reporting at home.
whatHurts: Severe symptoms that go unanswered, patients who give up on a service meant to protect them, and nurses handling alert volumes without a weekend rota.
currentPractice: Weekly questions on a tablet or phone with automatic alerts to the triage nurse on weekdays; usual telephone triage in the clinics not yet started; no routine measure of completion or alert response time.
whyNow: Two more clinics start in January 2027, the rollout committee has committed to offering reporting to every patient by mid-2027, and the platform can only be reconfigured at the June 2027 update.
constraints: No research funding; the nurse specialist has one protected day a week until December 2027. Interviews must happen during clinic hours or by telephone. The reporting platform cannot be reconfigured before the vendor update in June 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Every patient who reports a severe symptom gets a timely response, and patients who cannot or will not report electronically still have a safe route.
summary: Problem framed around completion and alert response in routine care; the choice between a trial and a mixed methods evaluation is left to the design stage.
